Earliest listed publication among matched versions, not proof of an unedited contemporaneous archive. Claim timestamps refer to the reviewed version.

## Summary

The June 20 wrap is cautious on solar and homebuilders, while distinguishing weak housing demand from a mortgage credit crisis. Eisman again declines to call private credit a bubble, but overstates how little credit-quality information exists. His core tool is to separate the growth of lending from the quality of the loans.

The housing affordability and incentive diagnosis has strong support. The solar view is conditional on policy and should not be treated as a fixed 2029 short. His mortgage-payment arithmetic and blanket private-credit data assertion need correction.

## Material claims

<a id="youtube-Ni_Zlf9Iw08-c002"></a>
### 002. Iran and trade policy are the principal near-term market risks, and a trade war could cause recession.

**Not testable** | Steve Eisman | forecast | major

[Source at 2:34-3:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ni_Zlf9Iw08&t=154s) | Stance: conditional | Horizon: not stated

The conditional scenario has no tariff threshold, recession deadline or isolated causal test. Calling the Fed irrelevant is rhetoric, not an independently demonstrated mechanism.

<a id="youtube-Ni_Zlf9Iw08-c003"></a>
### 003. The Senate proposal would shorten wind and solar incentives while retaining more support for nuclear, hydro and geothermal.

**Unresolved** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 3:53-4:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ni_Zlf9Iw08&t=233s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The final law has project-specific transition rules. The exact June proposal version was not independently recovered, so it is not graded against later legislation.

Assessment test: Compare the dated proposal with the enacted text.


<a id="youtube-Ni_Zlf9Iw08-c004"></a>
### 004. Residential solar economics have deteriorated with higher financing rates and adverse policy, and a durable sector rally needs a policy reversal.

**Unresolved** | Steve Eisman | investment thesis | major

[Source at 4:41-6:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ni_Zlf9Iw08&t=281s) | Stance: conditional | Horizon: not stated

The affordability mechanism is clear, but the sector, rally threshold and required policy change are not defined. The final law differed from the June proposal, so later rallies cannot fairly be scored as a clean unchanged-policy falsification.

Qualification: He says either a change of administration or a policy change; the first condition is not the only possible catalyst.

Assessment test: Compare residential solar financing, installations and a specified total-return index across actual policy changes.

- [Clean electricity credits after the 2025 law](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i7211) (None): Wind and solar termination rules include construction-start and placed-in-service exceptions. The final law is not identical to every June proposal and does not terminate every project credit on one date.

[Source at 6:34-7:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ni_Zlf9Iw08&t=394s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

Directionally consistent with company reports, but the spoken historical low mixes headline and regional/component series. An exact series comparison is needed.

<a id="youtube-Ni_Zlf9Iw08-c006"></a>
### 006. Current housing weakness is primarily affordability and mortgage-rate lock-in, not a repeat of subprime credit deterioration.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 7:08-7:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ni_Zlf9Iw08&t=428s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

FHFA research supports lock-in and OCC servicing data show a high current-loan share. These support the distinction, while not guaranteeing every borrower is sound.

Assessment test: Track affordability, listings, delinquencies and underwriting separately.

- [The Lock-In Effect of Rising Mortgage Rates, Working Paper 24-03](https://www.fhfa.gov/research/papers/wp2403) (2024-03-18): Primary loan-level research estimates higher market rates relative to existing loans reduce sale probability. Original abstract estimates 1.33 million prevented sales in 2022Q2-2023Q4 and upward price pressure from reduced supply. Estimates support the mechanism, not every December 2025 market statistic.
- [Mortgage performance in second-quarter 2025](https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/news-releases/2025/nr-occ-2025-91.html) (None): Within the covered servicer sample, 97.5% of loans were current and performing at quarter-end, versus 97.3% a year earlier. The sample does not cover every US mortgage.

<a id="youtube-Ni_Zlf9Iw08-c007"></a>
### 007. Moving from a 3% mortgage to 7% requires roughly halving the home price to keep the same payment.

**Wrong** | Steve Eisman | explanation | supporting

[Source at 7:37-7:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ni_Zlf9Iw08&t=457s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

For a fixed 30-year amortizing principal-and-interest loan, the affordable principal falls about 36.6%, not 50%. Taxes, insurance and down payments change the full household calculation.

Conditional reasoning: Monthly payment factor is r/(1-(1+r)^-360). Factors at 3% and 7% are approximately 0.004216 and 0.006653, so new principal is 0.6337 of old principal.

Assessment test: Hold loan term and monthly principal-and-interest payment constant.


<a id="youtube-Ni_Zlf9Iw08-c008"></a>
### 008. Large builders have stronger business models than before the GFC, but incentives are eroding current margins.

**Mixed** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 8:01-8:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ni_Zlf9Iw08&t=481s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

Lennar confirms significant incentive and margin pressure. Better land and financing practices are plausible but vary by builder and do not establish uniform financial strength across the group.

Assessment test: Compare land commitments, leverage, cash flow and incentive-adjusted margins by builder.

- [Lennar second-quarter 2025 results](https://investors.lennar.com/press-releases/2025/06-16-2025-224524472) (2025-06-16): The release reports lower selling prices, substantial incentives and compressed homebuilding margins. This supports operating pressure, not a return forecast for the shares.

<a id="youtube-Ni_Zlf9Iw08-c011"></a>
### 011. There is no credit-quality data for private credit because all these lenders are private.

**Wrong** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 11:11-12:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ni_Zlf9Iw08&t=671s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The discussion includes BDCs, and public direct lenders already disclosed non-accruals, credit grades and realized losses. Partial visibility is not zero visibility.

Assessment test: Inspect BDC filings and identify which private funds remain unobserved.

- [Ares Capital Q1 2025 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1287750/000128775025000018/arccq1-2025exhibit991.htm) (2025-04-29): The public direct-lender release disclosed non-accrual balances, portfolio credit grades and realized losses before this episode. It does not provide complete data for all private-credit funds.

<a id="youtube-Ni_Zlf9Iw08-c012"></a>
### 012. The GFC was unusual because bad credit helped cause recession; normally recession produces credit losses.

**Mixed** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 12:28-13:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ni_Zlf9Iw08&t=748s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The FCIC supports the GFC credit mechanism, but a universal normal-cycle direction of causality is too simple because credit supply and real activity interact.

Assessment test: Separate the initiating shock, lending contraction and realized losses in each cycle.

- [Financial Crisis Inquiry Report, findings and chapters 4, 6, 7, 13](https://fcic-static.law.stanford.edu/cdn_media/fcic-reports/fcic_final_report_full.pdf) (2011-01-27): Investigative evidence documents fragile leverage/funding, fee and ROE incentives, deteriorating underwriting, and securitization dependence. Pages 61-64 describe pay incentives; pages 89 and 125 describe the origination chain; page 281 reports Bear near 38:1 and balance-sheet window dressing. Findings are not proof of a single exclusive cause.

<a id="youtube-Ni_Zlf9Iw08-c013"></a>
### 013. Private-credit problems will emerge in the next recession, but will not cause that recession.

**Not testable** | Steve Eisman | forecast | major

[Source at 12:49-13:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ni_Zlf9Iw08&t=769s) | Stance: conditional | Horizon: not stated

The episode specifies neither the next recession date nor what qualifies as a systemic private-credit problem. This is a conditional causal view, not a dated crash forecast.

Assessment test: Define recession, loss severity and causal transmission before evaluating.


## Framework and tools

- Separate housing demand from mortgage default risk.
- Trace subsidies and financing rates through customer affordability.
- Follow loan quality as well as loan growth.
- Do not equate opacity with demonstrated fraud or a proven bubble.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- Builder margins and incentives
- Mortgage-rate lock-in
- Monthly-payment arithmetic
- Bank versus nonbank loan-growth charts
- Private-credit non-accruals
